Clifty Coal Power Plant, Madison, Indiana. Photo: Jeffrey St. Clair.

As projections of U.S. [electricity demand rise
sharply](https://www.energy.gov/articles/doe-releases-new-report-evaluating-
increase-electricity-demand-data-centers), President Donald Trump is looking
to coal – historically a [dominant force in the U.S. energy
economy](https://us-sankey.rcc.uchicago.edu/) – as a key part of the solution.

In an April 2025 executive order, for instance, Trump [used emergency
powers](https://www.energy.gov/ceser/does-use-federal-power-act-emergency-
authority) to [direct the Department of
Energy](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/strengthening-
the-reliability-and-security-of-the-united-states-electric-grid/) to order the
owners of [coal-fired power plants that were slated to be shut
down](https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/climate-energy/us-urges-
utilities-keep-coal-fired-plants-running-ai-demand-booms-energy-2025-09-25/)
to keep the plants running.

He also directed federal agencies to “[identify coal resources on Federal
lands](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/04/fact-sheet-president-
donald-j-trump-reinvigorates-americas-beautiful-clean-coal-industry/)” and
ease the process for leasing and mining coal on those lands. In addition, he
issued orders to exclude coal-related projects from environmental reviews,
[promote coal exports](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/04/fact-
sheet-president-donald-j-trump-reinvigorates-americas-beautiful-clean-coal-
industry) and potentially subsidize the production of coal as a national
security resource.

But there remain limits to the president’s power to slow the declining use of
coal in the U.S. And while efforts continue to overcome these limits and prop
up coal, mining coal remains an ongoing danger to workers: In 2025, there have
been [five coal-mining deaths](https://minesafety.wv.gov/historical-
statistical-data/fatal-accident-summaries/) in West Virginia and at [least two
others elsewhere](https://www.msha.gov/data-and-reports/fatality-
reports/search?combine=coal&field_mine_category_target_id=All&year=2025&location_node_administrative_area=All)
in the U.S.

**A long legacy**

Until 2015, coal-fired power plants [generated more electricity than any
other](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=43675) type of fuel in
the U.S. But with the rapid expansion of a [new type of hydraulic
fracturing](https://www.chicagobooth.edu/magazine/history-of-fracking),
natural gas became a cheap and stable source for power generation. The prices
of solar and wind power also dropped steadily. These alternatives ultimately
[overcame coal](https://www.forbes.com/sites/rrapier/2024/05/20/how-natural-
gas-and-renewables-dethroned-coal-in-america/) in the U.S. power supply.

Before this change, coal mining defined the economy and culture of many U.S.
towns – and some states and regions, such as
[Wyoming](https://www.wyohistory.org/encyclopedia/coal-business-wyoming) and
[Appalachia](https://appalachianmemories.org/2025/01/08/coal-camps-in-
appalachia-in-the-1940s-life-in-the-shadows-of-industry/) – for decades. And
in many small towns, coal-related businesses, including power plants, were
[key employers](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2024.124561).

Coal has both benefits and drawbacks. It provides a reliable fuel source for
electricity that can be [piled up on-site at power plants](https://www.power-
eng.com/coal/coal-stockpiles-at-plants-to-remain-healthy/) without needing a
tank or underground facility for storage.

But it’s dirty: Thousands of coal miners developed a disease called [black
lung](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/owcp/dcmwc/statistics/PartsBandCBeneficiaries).
The federal government pays for medical care for some sick miners and makes
[monthly payments to family members](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/owcp/dcmwc)
of miners who die prematurely. Burning coal also emits multiple air
pollutants, [prematurely killing half a million
people](https://news.utexas.edu/2023/11/27/coal-power-killed-half-a-million-
people-in-u-s-over-two-decades/) in the United States from 1999 through 2020.

Coal is dangerous for workers, too. Some coal-mining companies have had
abysmal safety records, leading to [miner deaths](https://www.msha.gov/data-
and-reports/fatality-reports/search), such as the recent [drowning of a
miner](https://www.post-gazette.com/business/powersource/2025/11/13/wv-coal-
mine-flooded/stories/202511130066) in a sudden flood in a West Virginia mine.
Safety reforms have been implemented since the [Big Branch Mine
explosion](https://www.msha.gov/data-reports/mine-disaster-
investigations-2000) in 2010, and coal miner deaths in the U.S. have since
declined. But coal mining remains a hazardous job.

**A champion of coal**

In both of his terms, Trump has championed the revival of coal. In 2017, for
example, Trump’s Department of Energy asked the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission to [pay coal and nuclear
plants](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2017/10/10/2017-21396/grid-
resiliency-pricing-rule) higher rates than the competitive market would pay,
saying they were key to keeping the U.S. electricity grid running. The
[commission
declined](https://nyisoviewer.etariff.biz/ViewerDocLibrary/FercOrders/20180108%20Ordr%20Trnmnt%20RM%20Intt%20Nw%20Prcdng_21291.pdf).

In his second term, Trump is more broadly using [powers granted to the
president in emergencies](https://theconversation.com/the-us-energy-market-
has-its-troubles-though-it-may-not-be-a-national-emergency-249336), and he is
seeking to subsidize coal [across the board](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-
sheets/2025/04/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-reinvigorates-americas-
beautiful-clean-coal-industry/) – in mining, power plants and exports.

At least some of the urgency is coming from the rapid construction of data
centers for artificial intelligence, which the [Trump administration
champions](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/07/fact-sheet-
president-donald-j-trump-accelerates-federal-permitting-of-data-center-
infrastructure/). Many individual data centers use as much power as a [small
or medium city](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/11/23/data-centers-powering-ai-
could-use-more-electricity-than-entire-cities.html). There’s enough generation
capacity to power them, though only by [activating power plants that are idle
most of the time](https://nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/publications/rethinking-
load-growth) and that operate only during peak demand periods. Using those
plants would require data centers to reduce their electricity use during those
peaks – [which it’s not clear they would agree to
do](https://www.devsustainability.com/p/why-dont-data-centers-demand-
response).

So many data centers, desperate for 24/7 electricity, are relying on [old
coal-fired power plants](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/fossil-fuel-gas-
coal-climate-data-centers/753565/) – buying electricity from plants that
otherwise would be shutting down.

**Limits remain**

Despite the Trump adminstration’s efforts to rapidly expand data centers and
coal to power them, [coal is more
expensive](https://www.forbes.com/sites/energyinnovation/2025/06/08/coal-
power-costs-soar-28-since-2021-rising-faster-than-inflation/) than most other
fuels for power generation, with costs still rising.

[Half of U.S. coal mines have
closed](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=48936) within the past
two decades, and [productivity at the remaining mines is
declining](https://www.eia.gov/coal/annual/) due to a [variety of
factors](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=64924), such as
rising mining costs, environmental regulation and competition from cheaper
sources. Coal [exports have also seen
declines](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=66524) in the midst
of the tariff wars.

The U.S. Department of the Interior’s recent effort to follow Trump’s orders
and lease more coal on federal lands received only one bid – at a historically
low price of [less than a penny per
ton](https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2025-10-07/company-bids-less-
than-a-penny-per-ton-in-biggest-us-coal-sale-in-over-a-decade). But in fact,
even if the government gave its coal away for free, it would still make more
economic sense for utilities to build power plants that use other fuels. This
is due to the [high cost of running old coal
plants](https://energyinnovation.org/report/the-coal-cost-crossover-3-0/) as
compared to new natural gas and renewable infrastructure.

[Natural gas is cheaper](https://www.lazard.com/research-insights/levelized-
cost-of-energyplus-lcoeplus/) – and, in some places, so are renewable energy
and battery storage. Government efforts to prevent the retirement of coal-
fired power plants and boost the demand for coal may slow coal’s decline in
the short term. In the long term, however, [coal faces a very uncertain
